newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Guess who's coming to lunch, Mrs Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Guess who's coming to lunch, Mrs Clinton.

text.p: U.S. First Lady and leading feminist Hillary Rodham Clinton came to talk to Australia's most prominent women about empowerment, a move she said on Thursday was central to the world's prosperity into the new century.
But even before she rose to speak at Sydney's famous Opera House, her appearance had stirred considerable debate -- over whom she would have for lunch.
Several prominent, and generally left-leaning, women were reportedly upset at being absent from the guest list for the small private lunch that Clinton had requested.
She had asked to meet about 30 high-profile Australian women involved in areas of deep interest to her, including health care, child welfare and discrimination.
Janette Howard, wife of Liberal Prime Minister John Howard, duly issued invitations in consultation with White House staff.
Included were Federal Court judge Catherine Branson, Affirmative Action Agency director Catherine Harris, and aboriginal leader Lois O'Donoghue.

But critics, including members of the opposition Labor Party, complained the list had been loaded with allies of the conservative Liberal-National government and that many women Clinton would like to meet had been shunned, including feminist author Anne Summers.
"I would like to know what Hillary Clinton is going to talke about with the Liberal women," said Sydney politician Faye Lo Po, another shunned leftwinger.
"It's not exactly a smorgasbord of talent."
Also originally ignored was the country's most prominent female political leader, Cheryl Kernot, who heads the influential Australian Democrats political party.
Kernot jetted into Sydney just in time for the lunch after the prime minister's office said her absence was an oversight.
Addressing a specially-invited audience after the lunch, Clinton urged greater attention to women's issues, saying feminist concerns were central to the world's prosperity into the new century.
"Will democracies on every continent come to understand that issues affecting women are not soft or marginal, but are central to the progress and prosperity of every nation?" she said.
